newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing bullish on defence, space activities.
newsitem.headline: Boeing bullish on defence, space activities.

text.p: The chairman and chief executive of U.S. aerospace giant Boeing Co on Friday gave an upbeat account of the company's outlook for defence and commercial space activities.

"The prospects for growth...will be some of the long-term development programmes like the Joint Strike Fighter (JSF)," Phil Condit told journalists on the last leg of a tour of five European countries in six days.
He said the commercial satellite launch market also provided ample scope for growth, adding that work on its Sea Launch maritime rocket joint venture was on target.

"Commercial space is going to be a growth market", Condit said. "That looks to be a very good and very interesting market with a lot of growth potential. There are more satellites in queue than there are launches available."
Boeing leads the $583 million Sea Launch project with a 40 percent share, and has as its partners RSC-Energia of Russia, Norway's Kvaerner and NPO-Yuxhnoye of the Ukraine.

Sea Launch is a modified oil platform for launching rockets bearing commercial satellites from a site in the Pacific Ocean. It will allow both Polar and Equatorial satellites launches, something not possible from current land-based sites, he said.
The launch platform and "mother ship" are nearing completion and will soon go for outfitting at Long Beach, California, he said.

But the European Arianespace consortium will remain the dominant player in the market, he said. Arianespace currently holds around half the commercial launch market with the Ariane 4 and will switch gradually to the heavier Ariane 5 rocket.

In military aircraft, the next-generation JSF is scheduled to start production in 2008, which will ensure long term work for Boeing. The JSF contract is potentially worth $200 billion. In the meantime, Condit said, Boeing will be building commercial aircraft in a world air travel market growing an annual five percent.

The planned merger with McDonnell Douglas (MDD) will reduce Boeing's dependence on economic cycles and airlines' capital spending plans by boosting the defence side, which is driven by "geopolitical" factors, he said.

Condit believed there would be funding to build both the JSF, which is scheduled to fly with the U.S. Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps, and the F22 combat plane, which is also under development. Industry observers have questioned whether the U.S. government would have money to fund both programmes.

Military procurement is moving away from judging products purely on performance grounds to consideration of value and cost, he said, adding that he thought the use of commercial manufacturing in its JSF proposal was key to its success.
Lockheed Martin is fielding a rival JSF concept.
The addition of MDD's defence activities will give Boeing a 40/60 percent split in respectively military and civilian sales, compared to a historic 20/80 percent share.
Condit said he would prefer 50/50 but added "60/40 is fine with me. I'm not going to do something to get to some number."
Boeing expects around $1 billion of savings from the MDD merger, mainly in cutting head office staff. Condit did not expect to make any disposals from the merger.
